...Careless.

I looked at the clock and muttered the failure to myself. Compared with the <ruby>instant before<rt>・・・</rt></ruby> when I last checked it, about twenty minutes had gone. Twenty minutes in which I had done nothing, nothing whatsoever, while my consciousness took a holiday to a place of its own choosing.

Lack of sleep was collecting its dues. Slacken the reins even a little, and my mind slips off like a boat with its <ruby>mooring<rt>mooring</rt></ruby> undone and goes drifting out to sea.

The manager and the others could not possibly have missed this disgrace. That they did not wake me was out of consideration, nothing else.

They know my family situation. Knowing it, they go on making quiet allowances.

I was grateful. But I could not lean on it. I am paid a salary, so work is owed against it. That responsibility is mine, full stop.

Nor is my household the only one suffering in these times. Every family has its burdens. The company is no exception. To put forward only my own suffering and pass the load to someone else's table is shamelessness of the first quality.
Self-correction was required.

The manager's pencil, which had been dancing along with a pleasant scratch-scratch, stopped dead. I pulled back my chair and stood up.

I went over to my colleague, who was staring out of the window, and followed her line of sight.

In front of the company entrance stood a crowd of people. Taken alone, that could have passed for a goods delivery.

But every one of them wore a dangerous expression, and each held a tube or a stick that looked even more dangerous. Not a delivery, then. Those implements are commonly called guns and swords.

In short, an armed gang had appeared in front of the company. A few employees stood nearby, unable to respond.

Not because they did not understand what was happening. The reverse, I think. They understood only too well who these people were and what they had come to collect.

They were bandits.

Their origin, nobody knew for certain. Guessing, however, was easy.

The truth is, armed plunder gangs of this kind are nothing rare in Yamato today. Overflowing, one could even say.

The storms of power struggle blowing inside and outside the Rokuhara Shogunate produce, naturally, as many losers as there are struggles. The loser loses his post and exits the political stage.

But exit from the stage does not necessarily mean exit from this world to Yomi. In most cases the two exits share one door. Some men, however, slip past the purge blade, find a side window, and go hiding in the countryside, planning a comeback.

They may have had convictions of their own. For the ordinary citizen, though, nothing is more inconvenient than a loser who refuses to die with dignity.

A man planning a comeback, or at least claiming so to hold his clan and followers together, cannot throw away his weapons. A man who keeps his weapons cannot mix into the town and earn an honest daily wage. So, as the means of living one day at a time, he arrives at the only road left: taking goods from citizens, with force standing behind him. Whatever the men themselves may claim, from outside no other name fits such a group but bandits. Thus they are born.

Places not much urbanized, beyond the Shogunate's easy reach, often became their hideouts. This town, unfortunately, had fitted the pattern.

Naturally we contacted the Shogunate and requested action. The reply was nothing at all. Not even a refusal. A refusal, at least, is a letter.

The Shogunate has no policy of leniency toward such soldiers-turned-thieves, mind you. Suppression does take place. But its strength is limited, and limited strength naturally goes first to enemies of higher danger.

Men who left office with a large army still in hand, men with popular support, men connected to foreign powers: these were marked for quick suppression. The people who had appeared in our town were none of these.

If anything, they were on the smaller side. Even so, they had enough force to make a country town shrink completely.

Too small to catch Rokuhara's attention, big enough to do banditry properly. Seen one way, we may have drawn the worst variety on the list.

Had the Shogunate been relatively stable and its army sitting idle, a clearing unit might possibly have been sent even to a town like ours. Unfortunately, this was not that time.

Rumor was spreading that Horigoe Kubo <ruby>Morimasa Ashikaga<rt>Morimasa Ashikaga</rt></ruby> would join hands with Chinjufu Shogun Yoritsuna Okabe and raise an army to topple Supreme Commander Moriuji Ashikaga. And Morimasa made no effort to explain himself, so Kamakura Central had its nerves on edge.

The three Kubo offices of Sasagawa, Oyumi and Koga, and Kamakura's central army, were all on alert for Horigoe's rising. Chasing small-time bandits was beyond them. Send any number of requests, none could pass.

Such being the circumstances, the bandit band occupying the mountain near town was enjoying an out-of-season spring.

かといえば、必ずしもそうではない。

の刃を逃れ、再起を期して野に潜るような者もいる。

　彼らには彼らなりの信念があったのかもしれない。

くれない事ほど迷惑な話も他になかった。

張して一族郎党を繋ぎ止める――以上、武器を捨てる
筈がなく、武器を手にしている以上、市井に混じって

In fact the manager was not a fool. He had the intelligence to see through everything I had just muttered to my colleague.

en.html:
Our Minato household is a branch of that house. However, I must say it is a little different in nature from the common branch family, which arises as the result of settling an inheritance problem.

Its origin is five hundred years ago, that is, nearly the same time the senior Minato house appeared. In fact the senior house was a party that came to this land on an imperial order, to seal the <ruby>evil thing<rt>・・・・・</rt></ruby>.

As the concrete method, they split the clan, set up a separate house, and had it perform rites to pacify the <ruby>evil<rt>evil</rt></ruby> thing, while the senior house guarded and watched over it. <ruby>That<rt>namely</rt></ruby> separate house is the Minato household.

Families specialized in such rites often stress purity of blood and repeat marriages among relatives. In the Minato household it went exactly the opposite way, probably because what they were set to guard was a harm.

The head of the Minato household was always a woman, and she always took a husband from outside the land to leave descendants. By constantly adding the blood of strangers, the household was made a foreign body, isolated along with the calamity it held.

The estate was always placed away from the village, for the same reason. High status was acknowledged, but the household was never allowed to melt into the land. Respected, and kept at a distance.

...That too has been an empty shell for long. The senior house, stubbornly conservative as traditional ruling classes always are, never neglects its arrangements, and so the <ruby>shell<rt>form</rt></ruby> is maintained. But the awareness of the townspeople is already different from the past.

Most people see the Minato house as only a slightly unusual <ruby>local shrine<rt>・・・・</rt></ruby>. Otherwise, in this bandit matter, my foster mother could not have been propped up as a brake on the strong-minded senior house.

That was, to a good degree, due to my foster mother's elder-sister nature. Whatever the reason, for the senior house it must be displeasing on many layers.

So, going to meet the Head, I had steeled myself, at least to some extent.

　発祥は五百年前、つまり皆斗本家の登場とほぼ時を
同じくする。
　そもそも皆斗家は朝廷より勅命を受け、<ruby>あしきもの<rt>・・・・・</rt></ruby>
を封じるためにこの地へやって来た一党であった。

建て、〝<ruby>邪<rt>あ</rt></ruby>しきもの〟を鎮める祭祀を行わせ、本家が
それを警護及び監視する――という形をとった。
　<ruby>即<rt>すなわ</rt></ruby>ちその別家が、湊斗家である。

　このような祭祀に特化された家系は、血統の純潔を
重視し、親族婚を重ねる例が少なくない。
　湊斗家において、それがまさしく正逆になったのは、
役目として鎮守するものが悪害であったからだろう。

　湊斗家の当主は代々女性が務め、必ず外の土地から
婿を迎えて後裔を残した。
　常に他所者の血を加え続けることで、湊斗家を異類
の存在とし、抱える厄災もろとも隔離したわけである。

　屋敷地が常に里から離れた場所に置かれたことも、
理由は等しい。
　湊斗家は高い地位を認められながら土地に溶け込む
ことを許されず、敬して遠ざけられる立場にあった。

　……だがそれも、形骸化して久しい。
　伝統的支配層の常として頑迷なまでに保守的である
皆斗本家が手配りを怠らず、そのため<ruby>形骸<rt>かたち</rt></ruby>は維持され
続けているものの、町の人々の意識は既に過去と違う。

　大半の人は湊斗の家を、ちょっと変わった<ruby>お宮さん<rt>・・・・</rt></ruby>
程度にしか見ていなかった。
　でなければ山賊問題に際して、強気な本家への抑止
役に養母が持ち上げられることもなかったろう。

　それは多分に、姉御肌と呼ぶべき養母の性格のせい
でもあったろうが。
　何にしろ、本家にしてみれば幾重にも面白からぬ話
に違いない。

　だから会いに行くにあたり、それなりの覚悟はして
いた。

I did not know how to answer, and only lowered my eyes in a bow. Somewhere, from someone, I had heard that when my foster father took me in, the strongest opponent was this very conservative old man in front of me, so I had no <ruby>means<rt>means</rt></ruby> of reacting.

But the Head had not invented facts and praised my parents now, after the fact, to prop up his hard line. The people who gave me flesh and blood were, it seems, truly that kind of people.

They were from Narutaki, Nagasaki. That is, people of the Netherlands City-State, and in the strict sense not Yamato people.

Early in the 1800s by the foreign calendar, in the Napoleonic Wars that dragged in the whole of Europe, the <ruby>Kingdom of Holland<rt>Holland</rt></ruby> was trampled by the <ruby>British Commonwealth<rt>Britain</rt></ruby> and vanished from the earth. After the war ended, the land was not restored.

The plight of the Dutch, left with nowhere to go, soon reached the Tokugawa Directorate. Considering the long relations since the founding of the government, it concluded that to overlook it would be a betrayal of the nation's good faith.

It opened land near Nagasaki, then an international port and familiar to the Dutch, and gave it as a place to live. Dutch merchants and diplomats stuck in trading posts all over Asia, naturally, rushed in.

That land was named the Netherlands City-State, and was treated as an independent nation only by the Tokugawa Directorate and a few countries unfriendly to the British Commonwealth. Since then, one hundred years.

The little state of Narutaki village in Nagasaki slowly changed from its original character as a Dutch government in exile, and became something like a refuge for Europeans who had broken away from British rule. My ancestors too were of the kind who <ruby>sought refuge there<rt>・・・・・</rt></ruby>.

By what I was told, in my grandfather's generation they crossed from the <ruby>New World<rt>Neo-Britain</rt></ruby>. Probably they were defeated soldiers of the Second New World War of Independence.

'<ruby>Our Great Homeland<rt>Our America</rt></ruby>' must be freed from the <ruby>Empress's<rt>Britain</rt></ruby> <ruby>yoke<rt>yoke</rt></ruby>—
That is the password still whispered in the New World today, they say. Perhaps my grandfather also said it.

...About my real relatives, things get vague. I carried my birth surname, an English surname that the founder, who wished to naturalize in Yamato, had <ruby>adapted<rt>arranged</rt></ruby> into Yamato style, and called myself <ruby>Jirou Arata<rt>Jirou Arata</rt></ruby> for only a few years after birth.

About twenty years ago, my father and mother of the <ruby>Arata<rt>Arata</rt></ruby> family, both, I am told, <ruby>of mixed ancestry<rt>hybrid</rt></ruby> with strong Yamato blood as well, left me behind as a small child, threw themselves into the continental front and died. This is not a rare story for people of Narutaki.

The wish to repay Yamato for taking them in must have been strong. The wish for revenge on the British Commonwealth, spreading its net of rule from Europe into Asia, must also have been there. Adults of Narutaki, men and women alike, joined the Yamato army in large numbers.

Many also joined the Netherlands Knights Order, formed inside the city-state. Four years ago, at the end of the last war, this order sortied to the Kyushu front, fought fiercely against the League army, and was annihilated.

In the army my parents had, it seems, been friends with my foster father. Because of that connection, he took me in.

Since then, more than twenty years, I have lived as the adopted son of the Minato house, Kageaki Minato.

Today the Netherlands City-State officially does not exist. The League of Nations declared that it does not recognize it as a nation, and placed it under the strict watch of the League army. I have not heard of any persecution, but living conditions must be hard.

When I imagine how hard it would be to live there as an orphan with no parents, my foster father's kindness is something I must thank him for many times over. And the family that took me in along with him.

I am in debt to the Minato house.

〝<ruby>偉大なる故郷<rt>アウァ・アメリカ</rt></ruby>〟を<ruby>女帝<rt>ブリテン</rt></ruby>の<ruby>軛<rt>くびき</rt></ruby>から解放せよ――
　今も新大陸で密やかに叫ばれているという合言葉を、
祖父も口にしたのではないか。

　……実の親族の事は、どうにも曖昧になる。
　俺が生家の姓――大和への帰化を志した家祖が本来
の英語姓を和風に<ruby>改変<rt>アレンジ</rt></ruby>したもの――を冠し、<ruby>改次郎<rt>あらたじろう</rt></ruby>と
名乗っていたのは生後ほんの数年ばかりに過ぎない。

　およそ二十年前、<ruby>改<rt>アラタ</rt></ruby>家の父と母――二人とも大和人
の血をも濃く備える<ruby>混血<rt>ハイブリッド</rt></ruby>であったそうな――は、幼児
だった俺を残し、大陸戦線に身を投じて戦死した。
　これは長崎鳴滝の人間として珍しい話ではない。

　流亡の身を迎え入れてくれた大和の恩に報いる想い
が強かったのだろう。欧州からアジアへと支配の網を
広げてゆく大英連邦に対する復仇の意欲もあったろう。
　長崎鳴滝の成人は男女問わず多くが大和軍に参じた。

　また、市国内で結成されたネーデルラント騎士団に
加わる者も多かった。
　これは四年前――先の大戦末期に九州最前線へ出撃
し、連盟軍相手に奮戦、玉砕を遂げている。

　軍内で、俺の両親は養父と親交があったらしい。
　その縁で、養父は俺を引き取ってくれたのだ。

　それから二十年余の歳月を、俺は湊斗家の養子――
湊斗景明として生きている。

　現在、ネーデルラント市国は公的には存在しない。
　国際連盟に国家として認めない旨を宣告されたうえ、
連盟軍の厳重な監視下に置かれている。弾圧まで受け
ているとの報は聞かないが、生活環境は厳しかろう。

　そんな中で、親なしの孤児として生きる至難を想像
すれば、養父の厚意は俺にとって幾重にも感謝せねば
ならぬものだった。
　養父と共に俺を受け入れてくれた一家にも。

　俺は、湊斗の家に恩義がある。

The Head fell silent. His face was twisted with anger he could not contain, and had become terrifying.

This is a danger signal. Everyone who is close to the Head and knows him, on seeing this face, drops everything at once and retreats, because otherwise they themselves become the outlet for his anger.

In this district, that could mean social ruin. People who carelessly triggered the Head's outburst, lost their jobs and ended up on the road were not one or two.

But I could not run away.
Hikaru had no time left.

The next fit might take her life. Or maybe the one after that. What was certain was that it could not go on forever, and that the end was far closer to nothing than to eternity.

There was no room to watch the Head's mood.
I prostrated myself on the spot.
